No slides were found for this lecture. The page is built from the doctor's notes (green), every gift (red) and the Aldughaither summary (grey, at the end).

Core concept

  • Order of the lecture: embryology → anatomy → physiology → evaluation → inflammatory/benign disease → nodules/goitre → malignancy → treatment and follow-up.
  • Two cell types, two different cancers: follicular cells make T3/T4 and keep iodine uptake/TSH response (→ RAI works); parafollicular C cells (ultimobranchial body) make calcitonin → medullary carcinoma, which does not respond to RAI.
  • Thyroid neoplasm from the parafollicular C cells → medullary carcinoma. 429 ×3

Embryology

  • Follicular tissue starts at the foramen caecum (base of tongue) and descends to the pretracheal position, attached by the thyroglossal duct (normally obliterates). C cells come from the ultimobranchial body.
  • Parathyroids develop from the pharyngeal pouches and migrate → ectopic sites (mediastinal, intrathyroidal) — a "missing" gland may be ectopic.
  • Thyroglossal duct cyst: midline neck mass, often in childhood, may get infected; moves with swallowing AND with tongue protrusion — always test both.
  • 12-year-old girl, midline neck mass moving with swallowing and tongue protrusion → Sistrunk procedure (cyst + tract + middle third of the hyoid). 437 ×4
  • Lingual/ectopic thyroid: failure of descent; can obstruct the airway. Before removing it, confirm a normally placed cervical thyroid (US) — it may be the only thyroid tissue.
  • Pyramidal lobe ≈ 50% of people (normal variant). Agenesis — not a surgical disease.

Anatomy

  • ~15–25 g, butterfly-shaped, normally not palpable, highly vascular. A goitre can descend behind the sternum → retrosternal goitre.
ArteryOrigin
Superior thyroidExternal carotid
Inferior thyroidThyrocervical trunk (subclavian)
Thyroid ima (inconstant)Brachiocephalic trunk / aortic arch
VeinDrains to
Superior & middle thyroidInternal jugular
Inferior thyroidBrachiocephalic
  • Nerves at risk in thyroidectomy → recurrent laryngeal + external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. 439 ×5

Physiology

  • Follicular cells take up iodine, make, store and secrete hormone — mostly T4; T3 is more active. TRH → TSH → thyroid; hormones feed back negatively.
  • TSH stimulates iodine uptake → high TSH improves RAI uptake. Differentiated cancers keep this function — hence "differentiated".
  • Tests: TSH + free T4 (T3 if hyperthyroidism suspected with normal T4).
  • Calcitonin (C cells) inhibits osteoclastic resorption → modestly lowers calcium (minor compared with PTH).
  • Mechanism that lowers plasma calcium → calcitonin acting on the kidneys (↑ calcium excretion) — PTH and vitamin D raise calcium. 437 ×3

Evaluation

  • History: hyper/hypothyroid symptoms, neck mass, compressive symptoms (dysphagia, dyspnoea worse lying down), voice change, previous radiation, family history.
  • Examine thyroid + cervical nodes; mobility with swallowing; tongue protrusion for congenital masses.
  • TFTs ± antibodies (Graves).
ImagingRole (doctor)
UltrasoundStandard first-line thyroid imaging
CTSelective: retrosternal extension, invasion, deep/mediastinal disease, node mapping
Uptake scanFunction, not morphology — for hyperthyroid states, not cancer diagnosis
  • Cough + mild dysphagia, enlarged right lobe → CT neck and chest (retrosternal extension) 438 ×12; neck mass moving with swallowing + dyspnoea and dysphagia → retrosternal thyroid. 438

Hypo- & hyperthyroidism

  • Hypothyroidism alone is NOT an indication for surgery — only with another indication (compressive goitre, suspicious nodule).
  • Hypothyroid patient for elective lap chole → postpone until euthyroid 438 ×2; hypothyroid patients risk myxoedema coma after surgery. 438
  • Hyperthyroidism: ↓TSH, ↑T3/T4 — weight loss, heat intolerance, sweating, diarrhoea, menstrual disturbance; untreated → thyroid storm.
  • Graves: autoimmune, diffuse; stimulating antibodies. Ophthalmopathy worsens with smoking and with RAI → significant eye disease favours thyroidectomy.
  • Surgery favoured by: large/compressive goitre, significant ophthalmopathy, failed medical therapy, poor compliance, drug side-effects, young patient wanting definitive therapy, pregnancy (when medical/RAI unsuitable), suspicion of cancer.
  • Graves is diffuse → total thyroidectomy (never leave one side).
  • Toxic nodule → disease in one lobe → hemithyroidectomy/lobectomy if surgery is indicated. Thyroid surgery should be an anatomical hemi- or total thyroidectomy — never enucleation.
  • Woman of childbearing age with a hot (toxic) nodule → keyed antithyroid medication (RAI avoided if planning pregnancy; lobectomy is the definitive option). 434

Thyroiditis

TypeFeaturesManagement
Acute suppurativeRare bacterial, pus; painful swelling, fever; US collectionInfection treatment + drainage
Subacute (de Quervain)Painful, non-suppurative; tender; no collectionSelf-limited, no surgery
HashimotoAutoimmune → hypothyroidism; goitre; anti-TPO/anti-thyroglobulinSurgery only for large/compressive gland or suspicious lesion
RiedelExtensive fibrosis, constricts structuresSurgery for compression
  • Long-standing Hashimoto's + rapidly enlarging diffuse goitre with stridor → thyroid lymphoma. 435 ×7

Thyroid nodule & goitre

  • Approach: history + exam → ultrasound → TFTs → FNA when indicated.
  • US report: size, location, uni/bilateral, echogenicity, composition, margins, calcifications, vascularity, extension, cervical nodes.
  • Neck levels I–VII: level VI = central compartment (thyroid cancer's commonest nodal site); lateral neck = II–V; VII = superior mediastinum.
  • FNA is the gold-standard sampling for thyroid nodules (core biopsy only selectively).
  • Solitary nodule, normal TFTs, suspicious US → FNA cytology. 437 ×10
BethesdaMeaningMalignancy riskManagement
INon-diagnostic~1–4%Repeat US-guided FNA
IIBenign~3%Surveillance; surgery only for another indication (compression)
IIIAUS/FLUSIntermediateRepeat / further work-up
IVFollicular neoplasm~15–30%Molecular testing or diagnostic lobectomy
VSuspicious for malignancyHighSurgery
VIMalignant—By cancer type
  • 3-cm benign (Bethesda II) nodule with a choking sensation → hemithyroidectomy (compressive symptoms). 437 ×4

Thyroid cancer

  • Types: papillary, follicular, medullary, anaplastic, lymphoma, sarcoma, metastases. Papillary + follicular = "differentiated" (TSH-responsive, iodine uptake, thyroglobulin) → surgery, RAI, TSH suppression, Tg follow-up; excellent prognosis.
PapillaryFollicularMedullaryAnaplastic
Frequency~85%~10%Uncommon~1%
WhoYounger adults≥ 40~25% familial (MEN 2, RET)Elderly women (60s–70s)
SpreadLymphatic (nodes common)Haematogenous (vascular invasion)NodesEarly local invasion, metastases
Key pointBRAF; variants (tall cell, diffuse sclerosing); NIFTPFNA can't tell adenoma from carcinoma — needs capsular/vascular invasion on histologyCalcitonin, CEA; no RAIAll stage IV; palliative; survival > 2 y uncommon
Prognosis~96%Very goodWorseVery poor
  • Enlarged cervical nodes with a normal thyroid on exam in a 33-year-old → papillary carcinoma. 439 ×10
  • New name for the encapsulated (non-invasive) follicular variant of PTC → NIFTP. 442
  • Pre-treatment diagnostic marker (keyed) → calcitonin (medullary). 437 ×2

Medullary carcinoma & MEN 2

Before operating on MTC, rule out phaeochromocytoma (MEN 2). If present → treat the phaeo first, then the thyroid.
  • MEN 2: MTC + phaeochromocytoma + hyperparathyroidism (MEN 2A). Genetic testing of patient and family.
  • Treatment: total thyroidectomy + central (level VI) neck dissection — never a partial procedure; add lateral dissection when lateral nodes are involved.
  • Medullary carcinoma, 0.5-cm left nodule with enlarged left neck nodes → keyed total thyroidectomy + central neck dissection (the source notes ipsilateral lateral dissection is also needed — key follows the doctor). 439 ×2
  • Prophylactic total thyroidectomy is done for medullary carcinoma (RET mutation carriers). 435 ×5

Treating differentiated cancer

Tumor sizeExtent
< 1 cm (microcarcinoma)Lobectomy possible
1–4 cmLobectomy or total thyroidectomy by risk
> 4 cmTotal thyroidectomy (RAI needs all thyroid removed)
  • Favouring total thyroidectomy: bilateral disease, nodes, extrathyroidal extension, distant metastases, aggressive mutation, high risk, planned RAI.
  • RAI works only in iodine-avid tissue (differentiated cancers) after total thyroidectomy; indications: > 4 cm, nodes, extrathyroidal extension, metastases.
  • TSH suppression: levothyroxine at suppressive doses (not just replacement) — dose guided by TSH/free T4.
  • Thyroglobulin = tumour marker after total thyroidectomy ± RAI: a rising Tg = residual/recurrent disease (check anti-Tg antibodies). MTC follow-up = calcitonin + CEA.
  • Papillary cancer, long-standing swelling, euthyroid → keyed hemithyroidectomy. 437

Complications of thyroidectomy

  • Expanding neck haematoma with stridor 2 h post-op → open the wound and evacuate at the bedside 442 ×5; the most serious immediate complication in Graves' → neck haematoma. 441 ×2
  • Perioral tingling, cramps, Chvostek's → hypocalcaemia 441 ×3; treat with IV calcium gluconate 442; first action (keyed) → order a calcium level 437 ×3; numb fingers 2 weeks later → Chvostek's sign 435 ×6; labs keyed low Ca, low PTH (phosphate actually rises). 441
  • After total thyroidectomy: hypoparathyroidism, hypocalcaemia, hyperphosphataemia — not hypercalcaemia. 427 ×2
  • True statement about thyroidectomy risks → a parathyroid can be autografted (into the forearm or sternomastoid); bleeding is uncommon and neuropraxia is commoner than permanent nerve injury. 439

Other neck swellings (from past exams)

  • Elderly woman, 2-year swelling behind the mandible (parotid) → FNA. 426
  • Lateral neck mass with fever and sweating → TB work-up (PPD). 426
  • Swelling under the mandible, palpable in the mouth, pain on eating → submandibular gland stone. 426
  • Posterior triangle — posterior border → trapezius (anterior border sternocleidomastoid, base the clavicle). 426

Thyroid and Parathyroid

Thyroid:

Embryologic Development
  • Origin: The thyroid gland develops as a median endodermal downgrowth from the first and second pharyngeal pouches.
  • Migration Path:
  • Descends caudally from the foramen cecum (base of the tongue).
  • Merges with ultimobranchial bodies (from the fourth pharyngeal pouch), which contribute to parafollicular (C) cells (produce calcitonin).
  • Divides into two lobes upon reaching its adult position below the cricoid cartilage.
Clinical Correlations:
  • Thyroglossal Duct Cyst: Remnant of the thyroid’s migration path, presenting as a midline neck mass that moves with swallowing.
  • Lingual Thyroid: Ectopic thyroid tissue at the base of the tongue due to failure of migration.
  • Pyramidal Lobe: Present in 30-50% of individuals, extending superiorly from the isthmus.
Anatomy of the Thyroid Gland
  • Size & Weight: Normal weight 15-25 grams.
  • Location: Lies anterior to the trachea, just below the cricoid cartilage.
  • Structure:
  • Isthmus: Connects right and left lobes.
  • Lobes: Right and left, extending along the trachea.
  • Pyramidal Lobe (if present): Extends cranially from the isthmus.
Variants:
  • Unilateral Agenesis: More commonly affects the left lobe.

Vascular Supply

  • Arterial Supply:
  • Superior Thyroid Artery (from external carotid)
  • Inferior Thyroid Artery (from thyrocervical trunk)
  • Thyroid Ima Artery (variable, from the brachiocephalic trunk or aortic arch)
Clinical Relevance:
  • Thyroidectomy Complication: Ligation of the superior thyroid artery near its origin endangers the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (affecting cricothyroid muscle, leading to voice changes).
  • Inferior Thyroid Artery Ligature Risk: Proximity to the recurrent laryngeal nerve, increasing risk of hoarseness or vocal cord paralysis if injured.
  • Thyroid Ima Artery: Rare but significant—accidental injury can cause excessive bleeding.
  • Venous Drainage:
  • Superior Thyroid Vein → Internal Jugular Vein
  • Middle Thyroid Vein → Internal Jugular Vein
  • Inferior Thyroid Vein → Brachiocephalic Veins

Clinical Implications

  • Thyroidectomy:
  • Preserve parathyroid glands (vascularized by inferior thyroid artery).
  • Avoid recurrent laryngeal nerve injury (hoarseness or airway compromise).
  • Thyroid Goiter:
  • Can compress trachea & esophagus due to its location.
  • Retrosternal extension may require sternotomy for removal.
  • Congenital Thyroid Disorders:
  • Thyroglossal Duct Cyst requires Sistrunk procedure (removal of cyst + tract + central hyoid bone to prevent recurrence).
  • Ectopic Thyroid may be the only functional thyroid tissue—avoid resection without confirming normal thyroid tissue elsewhere.
Thyroid Gland: Function & Hormone Regulation
Primary Functions

The thyroid gland is responsible for the synthesis, storage, and secretion of the thyroid hormones:

  • Thyroxine (T₄)
  • Triiodothyronine (T₃)

These hormones play a crucial role in metabolism, growth, and development.

Thyroid Hormone Synthesis
1. Iodide Uptake:
  • Iodide (I⁻) is absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract.
  • Actively transported into thyroid follicular (acinar) cells via the sodium-iodide symporter (NIS).

2. Oxidation & Organification:

  • Iodide is oxidized to iodine (I₂) by thyroid peroxidase (TPO).
  • Iodine is incorporated into tyrosine residues within thyroglobulin (Tg) to form:
    • Monoiodotyrosine (MIT)
    • Diiodotyrosine (DIT)

3. Coupling Reactions:

  • MIT + DIT → T₃ (Triiodothyronine)
  • DIT + DIT → T₄ (Thyroxine)

4. Storage & Secretion:

  • T₃ and T₄ are stored in thyroid colloid within the follicle.
  • Upon stimulation, thyroglobulin is hydrolyzed, releasing T₄ and T₃ into circulation.
  • T₄ is the major secreted hormone, but 80% of T₃ is converted peripherally from T₄.
Thyroid Hormone Transport
  • Bound Form (99%):
  • Thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) (major carrier)
  • Transthyretin (TTR)
  • Albumin
  • Free Form (Active, <1%):
  • Only free T₃ and T₄ are biologically active.

Regulation of Thyroid Function The hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid (HPT) axis controls thyroid hormone levels via a negative feedback loop.

1. Hypothalamus:
  • Releases thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH).
  • Stimulates the pituitary gland.

2. Pituitary Gland:

  • Releases thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) (Thyrotropin).
  • TSH binds to TSH receptors on thyroid follicular cells.
  • Stimulates thyroid hormone synthesis & gland growth.

3. Thyroid Gland:

  • Secretes T₄ (major) and T₃ (minor).
  • Peripheral tissues convert T₄ → T₃ via 5’-deiodinase.

4. Negative Feedback:

  • High T₃/T₄ levels inhibit TRH & TSH release.
  • Low T₃/T₄ levels stimulate TRH & TSH production.
Clinical Correlation:
  • Hyperthyroidism (e.g., Graves' disease) → ↓ TSH due to excess T₄/T₃.
  • Hypothyroidism (e.g., Hashimoto’s thyroiditis) → ↑ TSH due to insufficient T₄/T₃.
Evaluation of the Thyroid Gland
1️- History & Physical Examination

A detailed history should include:

Systemic Symptoms:
  • Hyperthyroidism: Weight loss, heat intolerance, palpitations, tremors, anxiety.
  • Hypothyroidism: Fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, dry skin, constipation.
  • Local Symptoms: Hoarseness, dysphagia, dyspnea, neck swelling, pain.
  • Family History: Thyroid dysfunction (Graves', Hashimoto’s). Thyroid malignancies (medullary thyroid cancer & MEN syndromes).
  • Medication History: Lithium, amiodarone, iodine exposure.
Physical Examination Findings

Palpation of the Thyroid Gland assesses:

- Size & Contour: Diffuse enlargement vs. nodularity.

- Consistency: Soft (Graves’), firm (Hashimoto’s), hard (thyroid malignancy).

- Fixation to Surrounding Tissues: Suggests malignancy.

- Tracheal Deviation: Seen in large goiters.

- Cervical Lymph Nodes: Suggestive of thyroid cancer metastasis.

2️- Laboratory Tests
TSH (Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone)
  • Most sensitive test for thyroid function.
  • Differentiates hypothyroidism (↑TSH), euthyroidism (normal TSH), and hyperthyroidism (↓TSH).
Free T4 (FT4) & Free T3 (FT3)
  • FT4: Confirms primary thyroid dysfunction (hypo- or hyperthyroidism).
  • FT3: Useful for Graves' disease & T3 toxicosis.
Thyroid Antibodies
  • Anti-TPO (Thyroid Peroxidase Antibodies): Hashimoto’s thyroiditis.
  • TSH Receptor Antibodies (TRAb): Graves' disease.
Additional Tests
  • Thyroglobulin (Tg): Thyroid cancer monitoring.
  • Calcitonin: Medullary thyroid carcinoma screening (MEN2).
3️- Thyroid Imaging
Ultrasound (US)
  • First-line imaging for thyroid nodules & goiters.
  • Identifies solid vs. cystic nodules & malignant features (irregular borders, microcalcifications).
  • Assesses cervical lymph nodes for metastasis.
Radioactive Iodine Uptake Scan (RAIU)
  • Hyperthyroidism Workup: Diffuse uptake → Graves' disease. Focal "hot nodule" → Toxic adenoma. Low uptake → Thyroiditis, exogenous thyroid hormone use.
Fine Needle Aspiration (FNA)
  • Gold standard for evaluating thyroid nodules >1 cm (with suspicious ultrasound features).
  • Differentiates benign vs. malignant nodules.
Hyperthyroidism (Thyrotoxicosis)

Hyperthyroidism results from excess thyroid hormone production, leading to increased metabolic activity and sympathetic nervous system stimulation.

1️- Clinical Features
A. Symptoms & Signs
General:
  • Weight loss despite increased appetite
  • Heat intolerance, excessive sweating
  • Fatigue, muscle weakness
  • Increased bowel frequency, polyuria
Cardiovascular:
  • Tachycardia, palpitations
  • Atrial fibrillation
  • High-output heart failure
  • Cardiac flow murmur
Skin & Hair:
  • Warm, moist skin
  • Fine, thin hair
Neurological & Psychological:
  • Anxiety, nervousness, restlessness
  • Hyperreflexia
  • Shortened Achilles reflex time
Reproductive:
  • Menstrual irregularities, infertility
  • Gynecomastia in men
Ocular Signs (Graves' Disease):
  • Stare, lid lag
  • Exophthalmos (proptosis)
  • Periorbital edema
  • Conjunctivitis, diplopia
Goiter:
  • Diffuse, nodular, or solitary nodule
2️- Causes of Hyperthyroidism
A. Primary Hyperthyroidism (TSH ↓, T4/T3 ↑)
1. Graves’ Disease (Autoimmune):
  • Most common cause (TSH-receptor antibodies stimulate thyroid growth & function).
  • Often familial.
  • Thyroid bruit, pretibial myxedema, exophthalmos are specific to Graves'.

2. Toxic Multinodular Goiter (Plummer’s Disease)

  • Multiple hyperfunctioning nodules.
  • Common in older adults.

3. Solitary Toxic Adenoma

  • Single "hot" nodule on thyroid scan.

4. Subacute Thyroiditis (De Quervain’s Thyroiditis)

  • Post-viral, painful goiter, self-limiting.
  • Low iodine uptake.
B. Secondary Hyperthyroidism (TSH ↑, T4/T3 ↑)
  • TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma
  • hCG-secreting tumors (hydatidiform mole, choriocarcinoma)
  • Iodine-induced (Jod-Basedow effect) (e.g., amiodarone)
3️- Diagnosis
A. Laboratory Tests

TSH ↓ (best initial test)

T4 & Free T3 ↑

Thyroid-Stimulating Immunoglobulin (TSI) ↑ (Graves')

RAIU (Radioactive Iodine Uptake Scan):
  • High uptake → Graves' or toxic nodules.
  • Low uptake → Thyroiditis or exogenous thyroxine use.
4️- Differential Diagnosis
  • Anxiety disorder (normal thyroid function, persistent fatigue).
  • Atrial fibrillation (if no other hyperthyroid symptoms).
  • Pheochromocytoma (episodic palpitations, hypertension).
  • Myasthenia gravis (ophthalmoplegia but no thyroid dysfunction).
5️- Treatment Options
  • A. Antithyroid Medications
  • Methimazole (MMI) – 1st line, except in pregnancy.
  • Propylthiouracil (PTU) – Preferred in pregnancy (1st trimester).
  • Side effects: Rash, agranulocytosis, hepatotoxicity. B. Radioactive Iodine (I-131)
  • Definitive therapy for Graves' & toxic nodules.
  • Contraindicated in pregnancy & lactation.
  • Can cause hypothyroidism over time. Indications:
    • Recurrent hyperthyroidism
    • Patients who didn’t respond to medical therapy
    • Poor surgical candidates
  • C. Surgery (Thyroidectomy)
  • Indications:
    • Large goiter, obstructive symptoms
    • Malignancy suspicion
    • Ophthalmopathy
    • Pregnancy & Children
    • Amiodarone-induced hyperthyroidism
    • Risks: Hypoparathyroidism, recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.
6️- Graves’ Ophthalmopathy

Autoimmune inflammation of orbital tissues.

Management:
  • Steroids (1st line for severe cases).
  • Radiotherapy, decompression surgery for vision-threatening disease.
  • Avoid radioactive iodine (may worsen ophthalmopathy).
  • Smoking cessation (reduces severity).
Evaluation of Thyroid Nodules & Goiters

Thyroid nodules are common, but only ~10% are malignant. Proper evaluation aims to differentiate benign from malignant nodules and guide management.

1️- Risk Factors for Thyroid Cancer
Patient Characteristics:

Age: Higher malignancy risk in <20 years & >60 years Gender: Higher risk in males Family History:

  • Medullary Thyroid Cancer (MTC): ~25% familial (MEN 2A, MEN 2B)
  • Papillary Thyroid Cancer (PTC): Higher risk in Cowden, Gardner, & Carney syndromes
Environmental Factors:
  • History of Childhood Radiation Exposure (~40% develop thyroid cancer)
  • Iodine Deficiency or Excess
Nodule Features (Suspicious for Malignancy):
  • Rapid growth
  • Hard, fixed nodule
  • Hoarseness, dysphagia, dyspnea
  • Cervical lymphadenopathy
  • Cold nodule on RAIU scan
2️- Evaluation of Thyroid Nodules
A. History & Physical Exam

Assess duration, growth, local symptoms (dysphagia, voice changes) Palpation:

  • Hard, fixed nodule → Concerning for malignancy
  • Multinodular goiter (MNG) → Often benign
B. Thyroid Function Tests
TSH (Initial test)
  • ↓ TSH → Hyperfunctioning nodule (low cancer risk) → RAIU scan
  • ↑ or normal TSH → Proceed with ultrasound
T4, Free T3 (assess thyroid function)
3️- Imaging Studies
A. Ultrasound (Preferred Initial Imaging)

Determines size, shape, composition, vascularity

Suspicious Features (Suggestive of Malignancy):
  • Irregular margins
  • Microcalcifications
  • Hypoechoic appearance
  • Increased vascularity
  • Extrathyroidal extension
B. Radioactive Iodine Uptake (RAIU) Scan (If TSH is low)

"Hot" (Hyperfunctioning) Nodules → Benign, rarely malignant "Cold" (Nonfunctioning) Nodules → Higher cancer risk → FNA needed

C. CT/MRI (Advanced Cases)
Used for large, invasive, or substernal goiters
4️- Fine-Needle Aspiration (FNA) Biopsy
Indications:
  • ≥1 cm with suspicious ultrasound features
  • ≥1.5 cm if solid
  • ≥2 cm if purely cystic ✔ Bethesda System for Cytology Classification:
  • Benign (Category II) → Observation
  • Malignant (Category VI) → Surgery
  • Atypia/Follicular Lesion of Undetermined Significance (Category III) → Genetic testing or repeat FNA
False-Negatives: Higher risk in nodules >3 cm (sampling error)
5️- Management of Thyroid Nodules & Goiters
A. Benign Nodules

Small (<1 cm, asymptomatic): Observation, repeat ultrasound in 6-12 months Large, symptomatic, or growing nodules: Surgery or RAI therapy

B. Malignant Nodules

Papillary & Follicular Carcinoma: Thyroidectomy ± radioactive iodine Medullary Carcinoma: Total thyroidectomy (check for MEN 2A/2B)

C. Multinodular Goiter (MNG)
If asymptomatic → Observation
If compressive symptoms → Surgery
D. Non-Surgical Options

RAI Therapy: Used for toxic multinodular goiter Levothyroxine Suppression Therapy: Used selectively for benign nodules

6️- Indications for Thyroid Surgery
  • Malignancy or high suspicion of cancer
  • Indeterminate cytology with risk factors
  • Symptomatic (dysphagia, dyspnea, hoarseness)
  • Toxic nodule/goiter unresponsive to medical therapy
  • Cosmetic concerns (large goiter)
Simple or Nontoxic Goiter (Diffuse & Multinodular Goiter)

A goiter refers to an enlarged thyroid gland. A simple (nontoxic) goiter is not associated with hyperthyroidism or malignancy and typically results from compensatory thyroid enlargement due to inadequate hormone production or thyroid growth factors.

1️- Causes & Risk Factors
Physiologic Goiter
  • Normal in puberty & pregnancy
Endemic Goiter (Iodine Deficiency)
  • Common in iodine-poor regions
  • Compensatory TSH stimulation → Thyroid enlargement
Goitrogenic Substances
  • Foods: Cabbage, broccoli, soy, cassava
  • Drugs: Lithium, amiodarone
Autoimmune & Congenital Causes
  • Hashimoto’s Thyroiditis → Chronic inflammation, eventual hypothyroidism
  • Congenital defects in thyroid hormone synthesis
2️- Types of Nontoxic Goiter
A. Diffuse Nontoxic Goiter
  • Symmetric enlargement of the thyroid
  • Smooth surface
  • Usually euthyroid, but mild TSH suppression may occur
B. Multinodular Goiter (MNG)
  • Progressive nodular transformation of a longstanding goiter
  • Most common cause of thyroid enlargement in adults
  • Can be asymptomatic or cause compressive symptoms
  • Rarely progresses to hyperthyroidism (toxic multinodular goiter -
  • Plummer’s disease)
3️- Clinical Features
Symptoms
  • Neck pressure symptoms → Dyspnea, dysphagia
  • Venous congestion → Swelling in the neck, facial plethora
  • Thyroid function is usually normal
  • Compressive symptoms in large/substernal goiters
Physical Exam Findings
  • Diffuse smooth enlargement (early stages)
  • Nodular, asymmetric gland (later stages)
  • No tenderness or lymphadenopathy
4️- Diagnosis
  • TSH → Usually normal or slightly suppressed
  • Free T4 & T3 → Normal
  • Thyroid Ultrasound → Evaluates size, nodularity, and suspicious features
  • RAIU Scan (If TSH is low) → Helps differentiate from hyperfunctioning
  • nodules
  • Fine-Needle Aspiration Biopsy (FNA) → If nodules have suspicious features
  • CT/MRI → For substernal goiters or compressive symptoms
5️- Treatment & Management
A. Conservative Management
  • Asymptomatic patients → Observation, follow-up ultrasound
  • Levothyroxine suppression therapy → Considered in select cases
B. Indications for Surgery (Thyroidectomy)
  • Compressive symptoms (dyspnea, dysphagia, venous congestion)
  • Substernal goiter
  • Suspicious or rapidly growing nodules
  • Cosmetic concerns
C. Radioactive Iodine (RAI) Therapy
  • Used for large goiters in non-surgical candidates
  • Less effective for substernal goiters
Inflammatory Thyroid Disease

Inflammatory disorders of the thyroid gland are categorized as acute, subacute, or chronic thyroiditis and can be suppurative (infectious) or non-suppurative (non-infectious).

1️- Acute Suppurative Thyroiditis

Definition: A rare bacterial infection of the thyroid, often secondary to an upper respiratory tract infection (URTI).

Common Pathogens: Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, Pneumococcus, Coliform
bacteria

Associated with: Piriform sinus fistula (in recurrent cases)

Clinical Features
  • Severe neck pain with tenderness
  • Dysphagia, fever, chills
  • Erythema and swelling of the thyroid region
Diagnosis
  • Percutaneous aspiration, smear & culture → Confirms bacterial infection
  • Barium swallow (if recurrent) → Detects piriform sinus fistula
Treatment
  • IV antibiotics (based on culture results)
  • Surgical drainage (if abscess forms)
2️- Subacute Thyroiditis (De Quervain’s Thyroiditis)

Definition: A non-infectious, inflammatory thyroid disorder, often post-viral (e.g., after a flu-like illness).

Variants:
  • Painful subacute thyroiditis (classic De Quervain’s)
  • Silent thyroiditis (painless, needs differentiation from Graves’ disease)
Clinical Features
  • Neck pain radiating to jaw, chest, or ears
  • Fever, malaise, weight loss, palpitations
  • Transient hyperthyroidism → Followed by hypothyroidism, then recovery
Diagnosis
  • ↑ ESR & serum gamma globulin (hallmark feature)
  • ↓ Radioiodine uptake (RAIU) (vs. Graves’ disease which has ↑ uptake)
  • Normal or high thyroid hormone (T3/T4) levels
Treatment
  • NSAIDs (e.g., aspirin) or corticosteroids → Reduce inflammation
  • Beta-blockers → Manage hyperthyroid symptoms
  • Most patients recover within 2-6 months
3️- Hashimoto’s Thyroiditis (Chronic Autoimmune Thyroiditis)

Definition: The most common form of thyroiditis, caused by autoimmune destruction of thyroid tissue.

More common in: Women (~15% of U.S. women)
Clinical Features
  • Painless thyroid enlargement
  • Neck tightness, dysphagia (rare)
  • Hypothyroidism (in most cases, but may be transiently hyperthyroid
  • initially – Hashitoxicosis)
Diagnosis
  • ↑ Anti-thyroid peroxidase (TPO) & anti-thyroglobulin antibodies
  • Diffuse goiter with heterogeneous echotexture on ultrasound
  • Fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNA) if rapid growth or nodules are present
Treatment
  • Levothyroxine (LT4) for hypothyroidism
  • Surgery if → Compressive symptoms, suspicious nodules, or cosmetic
  • concerns
  • Complication:
  • Thyroid lymphoma → Rare but more common in Hashimoto’s patients
4️- Riedel’s Thyroiditis (Fibrosing Thyroiditis)

Definition: A rare fibrosing disorder of the thyroid gland with severe fibrosis & chronic inflammation.

Pathogenesis: Dense fibrotic infiltration replaces thyroid tissue and extends into surrounding structures.

Clinical Features
  • "Hard, woody" thyroid mass
  • Tracheal or esophageal compression → Stridor, dysphagia
  • Hypothyroidism & possible hypoparathyroidism
Diagnosis
  • Ultrasound & CT scan → Shows diffuse fibrosis
  • FNA biopsy or open biopsy → Confirms dense fibrosis
Treatment
  • Surgical decompression → For airway or esophageal obstruction
  • Glucocorticoids or tamoxifen → May slow progression

Benign Tumors of the Thyroid

Benign thyroid tumors are noncancerous growths of the thyroid gland. They include adenomas, cysts, and localized thyroiditis.

1️- Thyroid Adenomas

Definition: Encapsulated, solitary benign tumors arising from follicular thyroid cells.

Most common type: Follicular adenoma

Less common types: Hurthle cell adenoma, embryonal adenoma

Clinical Features
  • Solitary, slow-growing nodule
  • Usually painless and non-tender
  • May cause compression (if large) → Dysphagia, hoarseness
  • Rarely become hyperfunctioning ("toxic adenomas") → Hyperthyroidism
Diagnosis

Ultrasound: Well-defined, encapsulated lesion Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy: Cannot differentiate between benign follicular adenoma and follicular carcinoma → Requires surgical excision for

definitive diagnosis
Radioactive iodine scan:
  • "Cold" (non-functional) nodules → More likely to be malignant
  • "Hot" (hyperfunctional) nodules → Usually benign
Treatment
  • Observation (if small and asymptomatic)
  • Surgical excision → If suspicious for cancer, causing compressive
  • symptoms, or hyperfunctioning
2️- Thyroid Cysts

Definition: Fluid-filled nodules within the thyroid, usually benign Causes: Degeneration of adenomas, hemorrhage, or congenital

Clinical Features
  • Soft, fluctuant nodule
  • May rapidly enlarge if there is hemorrhage
  • Can cause compressive symptoms if large
Diagnosis
  • Ultrasound: Differentiates between solid vs. cystic nodules
  • FNA biopsy: Can drain the fluid and check for malignancy
Treatment
  • Aspiration (FNA) → If the fluid is clear and the nodule collapses, no further
  • treatment is needed
  • Surgical removal → If the cyst recurs or has suspicious features
3️- Localized Thyroiditis (Focal Nodular Hyperplasia)

Definition: Focal inflammatory lesion of the thyroid that can mimic a nodule Causes: Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, subacute thyroiditis

Clinical Features
  • Firm, irregular thyroid nodule
  • May be tender (especially in subacute thyroiditis)
  • Often associated with hypothyroidism (Hashimoto’s)
Diagnosis
  • Thyroid function tests (TSH, T3, T4)
  • FNA biopsy → Shows inflammatory cells
  • Ultrasound → Heterogeneous or hypoechoic lesion
Treatment
  • Depends on the underlying cause
  • Thyroid hormone replacement (if hypothyroid)
  • NSAIDs or steroids (if inflammatory)

Malignant Tumors of the Thyroid

Thyroid cancer is classified into different histologic types, each with varying degrees of aggressiveness and prognosis.

General Considerations
Common Clinical Features
  • Painless, enlarging thyroid nodule
  • Firm or hard, fixed mass
  • Dysphagia, hoarseness, or voice changes
  • Ipsilateral cervical lymphadenopathy
  • Normal thyroid function tests (most cases)
  • Cold nodule on radioiodine scan
  • Microcalcifications on ultrasound
Risk Factors
  • History of neck irradiation (childhood radiation, nuclear exposure)
  • Family history of thyroid cancer or multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN)
  • Iodine deficiency (follicular carcinoma)
  • Older age (>50 years for aggressive types like anaplastic carcinoma)
Types of Thyroid Cancer
1️- Papillary Carcinoma (85%) – Best Prognosis

Most common thyroid cancer (85% of cases)

Slow-growing, excellent prognosis
Spreads via lymphatics (regional lymph node metastasis common, distant
metastases rare)
Clinical Features
  • Painless, firm thyroid nodule
  • Palpable cervical lymphadenopathy (common in children and young
  • adults)
  • Microcalcifications on ultrasound (psammoma bodies)
  • Often multifocal within the thyroid
Pathology
  • Papillary architecture with psammoma bodies (microscopic calcifications)
  • BRAF mutation associated with more aggressive behavior
Treatment & Prognosis
  • Total or near-total thyroidectomy (if tumor >1 cm or bilateral)
  • Radioactive iodine (RAI) therapy (for high-risk patients)
  • TSH suppression therapy with levothyroxine
  • 10-year survival rate: >95%
2️- Follicular Carcinoma (10%) – Hematogenous Spread
Second most common thyroid cancer (10%)
More aggressive than papillary carcinoma
Spreads via bloodstream (hematogenous) → lungs, bones, liver
Associated with iodine deficiency
Clinical Features
  • Solitary, encapsulated thyroid nodule
  • No cervical lymphadenopathy (unlike papillary carcinoma)
  • Metastases to lungs, bones, or liver
Pathology
  • Follicular growth pattern
  • Capsular and vascular invasion distinguishes it from follicular adenoma
Treatment & Prognosis
  • Total thyroidectomy (for tumors >4 cm or invasive)
  • Radioactive iodine therapy (for metastatic disease)
  • 10-year survival rate: 80%-90%
3️- Hurthle Cell Carcinoma (Variant of Follicular Carcinoma)
Subtype of follicular carcinoma
More aggressive than typical follicular carcinoma
Does NOT take up radioactive iodine well
Clinical Features
  • Solitary, firm thyroid nodule
  • More common in older patients
  • Higher likelihood of cervical lymph node metastasis
Pathology
  • Hurthle cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm
  • Higher rate of vascular invasion than follicular carcinoma
Treatment & Prognosis
  • Total thyroidectomy
  • Less responsive to radioactive iodine therapy
  • 10-year survival rate: 50%-80%
4️- Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma (7%) – Produces Calcitonin
Derived from parafollicular C cells (not follicular cells)
Associated with MEN 2A and MEN 2B syndromes
Produces calcitonin → can cause hypocalcemia
Clinical Features
  • Solitary or multifocal thyroid mass
  • Flushing, diarrhea (due to excess calcitonin secretion)
  • Cervical lymphadenopathy (common)
  • Can be part of multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) syndromes
Pathology
  • Amyloid deposition within the tumor
  • Positive for calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA)
Diagnosis
  • Elevated calcitonin and CEA levels
  • RET proto-oncogene mutation testing (for MEN syndromes)
Treatment & Prognosis
  • Total thyroidectomy + central lymph node dissection
  • RAI is NOT effective (since tumor does not take up iodine)
  • 10-year survival rate: 50%-70%
5️- Anaplastic Thyroid Carcinoma (1%) – Worst Prognosis

Most aggressive and lethal thyroid cancer (median survival <6 months)

Occurs in older patients (>60 years)
Rapidly growing, invasive thyroid mass
Frequently invades the trachea → airway obstruction
Clinical Features
  • Rapidly enlarging, hard thyroid mass
  • Hoarseness, dysphagia, airway obstruction
  • Fixed mass with local invasion (trachea, esophagus, vessels)
Pathology
  • Poorly differentiated spindle or giant cells
  • High mitotic activity
Treatment & Prognosis
  • Surgery is usually not an option (due to extensive invasion)
  • External beam radiation + chemotherapy for palliation
  • 5-year survival rate: <5%

Treatment of Thyroid Cancer
1️- Differentiated Thyroid Carcinoma (Papillary & Follicular)

The main treatment for differentiated thyroid carcinoma (DTC) (papillary & follicular thyroid cancer) is surgical resection. The extent of surgery depends on the size of the tumor, presence of lymph node involvement, and risk factors.

Surgical Treatment Options
Thyroid lobectomy (for low-risk tumors):
  • Microcarcinomas (<1 cm) without risk factors
  • Small, well-differentiated tumors (1-4 cm) in low-risk patients
Total or near-total thyroidectomy (for high-risk tumors):
  • Tumors >4 cm
  • Presence of bilateral disease
  • Lymph node or distant metastases
  • History of radiation exposure or aggressive histologic features
Central Neck Dissection (CND):
  • Mandatory if central lymph nodes are positive
  • Prophylactic CND in high-risk patients is controversial
Lateral Neck Dissection:
  • Performed only if lateral neck lymph nodes are clinically involved
  • Modified radical neck dissection (preserving the jugular vein, sternocleidomastoid, and spinal accessory nerve)
Radioactive Iodine Therapy (RAI)
  • Given after total thyroidectomy in selected cases to destroy remaining thyroid cells or metastases
  • Indications:
  • Tumors >4 cm
  • Extrathyroidal extension
  • Lymph node metastases
  • Distant metastases
  • Not needed for:
  • Small low-risk papillary thyroid carcinoma
  • Localized, well-differentiated tumors <1 cm
TSH Suppression Therapy
  • Patients should be maintained on suppressive doses of levothyroxine (LT4) to reduce the risk of recurrence.
  • Low-risk patients: Maintain mild TSH suppression
  • High-risk patients: Maintain aggressive TSH suppression
Follow-Up & Surveillance
  • Serum thyroglobulin (Tg) is used as a tumor marker after total thyroidectomy.
  • Neck ultrasound is performed regularly.
  • TSH-stimulated thyroglobulin tests help assess recurrence.
Treatment of Metastatic Disease
  • Resectable distant metastases should be surgically removed if possible.
  • RAI therapy for iodine-avid metastases.
  • External beam radiation or targeted therapy (e.g., sorafenib, lenvatinib) for non-RAI-avid metastases.
2️- Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma (MTC)

MTC does not take up radioactive iodine, so treatment relies on surgery.

Surgical Treatment
Total Thyroidectomy + Central Neck Dissection
  • Mandatory due to high risk of lymph node metastases
  • Bilateral central neck dissection recommended
Lateral Neck Dissection
  • Performed if lateral lymph nodes are involved
  • Considered if calcitonin is highly elevated
Postoperative Surveillance
  • Serum calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) levels should be monitored every 6-12 months.
  • Persistent high calcitonin levels suggest residual or metastatic disease → Requires imaging (ultrasound, CT, PET scan).
Treatment of Advanced or Recurrent MTC
  • Targeted therapies (RET inhibitors) for advanced/metastatic MTC:
    • Cabozantinib
    • Vandetanib
  • Surgical debulking if feasible.
  • Liver metastases should be assessed via laparoscopy before further surgery.
3️- Anaplastic Thyroid Carcinoma (ATC)
Most aggressive thyroid cancer, poor prognosis
Rapid growth, airway compression, early metastases
Treatment Strategy
Palliative Surgery (if possible)
  • Debulking may help relieve airway obstruction, but cure is rare.
External Beam Radiation + Chemotherapy
  • Given to improve local control.
Targeted Therapy (BRAF/RET inhibitors)
  • Dabrafenib + Trametinib (if BRAF-mutant ATC)
Tracheostomy or Palliative Care
  • Often needed for airway obstruction.
  • Overall median survival <6 months.
